about: The Filliatreau family has farmed around the hamlet of Chaintres, just east of Saumur, for generations; they once grew asparagus and cereals alongside vines. In 1967 Paul Filliatreau took over from his father Maurice and became one of the first in the area to bottle his own wine. In 1978 he turned to stainless steel and short macerations, crafting a bright, fruit-driven Cabernet Franc that became a fixture of Parisian bistros and helped make Saumur-Champigny’s name. The family now farms about 50 hectares.

La Grande Vignolle is a single six-hectare plot on the limestone plateau above the cliff that runs along the Loire, at the northern edge of the appellation. Tuffeau quarried from this cliff in the 16th and 17th centuries built many of the Loire’s châteaux, and cave dwellings are still carved into it; the label shows the site. The vines average about 40 years old and are farmed biodynamically. Harvested by hand and destemmed, the fruit ferments with native yeasts over a 15-day maceration and spends a year in stainless steel.

It is bottled unfiltered, a request from the American importers Joe Dressner and Denyse Louis that the family still honours for the US market. The chalky soils give juicy, fresh Cabernet Franc: brambly dark berries and wild strawberry, with an undergrowth note the French call “sous bois.” With no oak to mask it, this is Cabernet Franc as the Saumur chalk shapes it.
facts: Single 6-ha plot on limestone above the Loire; vines about 40 years old
One year in stainless steel; unfiltered
